intake_baseline.high: I read a full chapter before pausing to review
intake_baseline.low: I pause after every few paragraphs to let it sink in

intake_baseline.high: I watch a 20-minute tutorial without stopping
intake_baseline.low: I stop the video every few minutes to process

working_memory_span.high: I keep track of several plot lines while reading a complex novel
working_memory_span.low: I lose track if a story has more than two main threads

working_memory_span.high: I can follow a multi-step recipe without re-reading the steps
working_memory_span.low: I need to re-read each step before doing the next one

processing_velocity.high: I understand the instructions for a new board game on the first read
processing_velocity.low: I need to read the rules twice before I get how to play

processing_velocity.high: I grasp a new math concept while the teacher explains it once
processing_velocity.low: I need to go over the examples again later to really get it

chunk_granularity.high: I prefer a project brief that gives the whole picture at once
chunk_granularity.low: I prefer a checklist that breaks the project into tiny tasks

chunk_granularity.high: I study for an exam by reviewing whole units in one go
chunk_granularity.low: I study by drilling one small section at a time

abstraction_tolerance.high: I understand a new coding concept from the syntax rules alone
abstraction_tolerance.low: I need to see a working code example before the rules make sense

abstraction_tolerance.high: I get the point of a philosophy essay without needing a real-life story
abstraction_tolerance.low: I need a concrete example to anchor a theoretical idea

example_density_need.high: I need to see several different problems solved before I try one myself
example_density_need.low: One worked example is usually enough for me to start practicing

example_density_need.high: I watch multiple tutorials on the same topic to see different approaches
example_density_need.low: I watch one good tutorial and then start trying it myself

text_density_tolerance.high: I read dense textbook pages without my mind wandering
text_density_tolerance.low: My focus drifts when a page has few breaks or pictures

text_density_tolerance.high: I prefer a long article with small print over a slide deck
text_density_tolerance.low: I prefer slides with bullet points over walls of text

vocabulary_ceiling.high: I read non-fiction books with specialized terms without a dictionary
vocabulary_ceiling.low: I keep a dictionary handy when reading books with technical terms

vocabulary_ceiling.high: I follow a lecture full of academic jargon without getting lost
vocabulary_ceiling.low: I zone out when a speaker uses too many unfamiliar words

jargon_absorption.high: I remember a new term after hearing it once.
jargon_absorption.low: I need to hear a new term several times before it sticks.

jargon_absorption.high: A single definition is enough for me to use a new word.
jargon_absorption.low: I have to look up a new word repeatedly to remember it.

spatial_anchoring.high: A diagram helps me understand a concept faster than text alone.
spatial_anchoring.low: I understand a concept faster by reading text than by studying a diagram.

spatial_anchoring.high: I grasp a process better when I can see its layout drawn out.
spatial_anchoring.low: Seeing a layout drawn out does not help me grasp a process better.

deductive_trajectory.high: I prefer learning a general rule before looking at specific examples.
deductive_trajectory.low: I prefer looking at specific examples before learning a general rule.

deductive_trajectory.high: Starting with the principle helps me make sense of the details later.
deductive_trajectory.low: Starting with the principle leaves me lost until I see the details.

inductive_trajectory.high: I understand a rule better after working through several cases first.
inductive_trajectory.low: Working through cases first leaves me confused about what the rule is.

inductive_trajectory.high: Seeing multiple examples helps me figure out the underlying pattern.
inductive_trajectory.low: Seeing multiple examples makes it harder for me to find the pattern.

cognitive_flexibility.high: I can switch between different ways of explaining the same idea.
cognitive_flexibility.low: I stick with the first explanation that makes sense to me.

cognitive_flexibility.high: If one mental picture fails, I easily try a different one.
cognitive_flexibility.low: If one mental picture fails, I have trouble finding another one.

analogical_transfer.high: A good analogy helps me grasp a difficult concept quickly.
analogical_transfer.low: Analogies usually distract me from grasping a difficult concept.

analogical_transfer.high: Comparing a new idea to something I know makes it click.
analogical_transfer.low: Comparing a new idea to something I know adds extra confusion.

causal_chain_depth.high: I can follow a long chain of cause-and-effect steps in my head.
causal_chain_depth.low: I lose track when a cause-and-effect chain gets longer than a few steps.

causal_chain_depth.high: I track multi-step consequences without writing them down.
causal_chain_depth.low: I need to write down multi-step consequences to keep them straight.

systems_thinking.high: I notice how changing one part of a project affects the others.
systems_thinking.low: I focus on each part of a project separately without linking them.

systems_thinking.high: I see how different topics in a course connect to each other.
systems_thinking.low: I treat different topics in a course as separate, unrelated units.

humor_receptivity.high: I remember the lesson better when the teacher cracks a few jokes.
humor_receptivity.low: Jokes during the lesson make it harder for me to focus on the content.

humor_receptivity.high: A funny example helps me understand a difficult concept more quickly.
humor_receptivity.low: Funny examples usually confuse me more than a straight explanation would.

narrative_pull.high: I pay closer attention when a new topic starts with a short story.
narrative_pull.low: I tune out when a lesson opens with a story before the facts.

narrative_pull.high: A case study helps me remember the theory better than a list of rules.
narrative_pull.low: Case studies feel like filler; I prefer going straight to the principles.

gamification_response.high: Seeing a streak counter makes me want to practice every single day.
gamification_response.low: Streak counters do not change how often I decide to practice.

gamification_response.high: Earning a badge for finishing a module gives me a real sense of progress.
gamification_response.low: Badges feel pointless; I track progress by what I can actually do.

challenge_appetite.high: I choose the hardest practice set because I learn more from struggling.
challenge_appetite.low: I pick the easier practice set so I can finish without getting stuck.

challenge_appetite.high: When a problem feels impossible, I keep trying different approaches for a while.
challenge_appetite.low: When a problem feels impossible, I move on and ask for the answer soon.

curiosity_hook.high: A puzzling question at the start makes me want to find the answer.
curiosity_hook.low: A puzzling question at the start just annoys me before the lesson begins.

curiosity_hook.high: I read further when a chapter opens with a mystery instead of a summary.
curiosity_hook.low: I prefer a clear summary at the start over a mystery hook.

interest_transfer.high: I understand statistics better when the examples use sports data I follow.
interest_transfer.low: Sports examples do not help me learn statistics any better than generic ones.

interest_transfer.high: Writing code for a game I like teaches me programming faster than textbook drills.
interest_transfer.low: Building a game project teaches me the same amount as standard coding exercises.

relevance_demand.high: I stop paying attention if I cannot see how the topic applies to real life.
relevance_demand.low: I keep learning a topic even if I do not see an immediate use for it.

relevance_demand.high: I need a concrete example of usefulness before I invest effort in a new skill.
relevance_demand.low: I will practice a new skill without needing a real-world example first.

tone_formality.high: I prefer textbooks that use precise, academic language throughout.
tone_formality.low: I prefer textbooks that explain things in casual, everyday language.

tone_formality.high: Formal lecture notes help me take the material more seriously.
tone_formality.low: Conversational lecture notes help me feel more comfortable with the material.

pattern_detection.high: I notice recurring structures in new material before anyone mentions them
pattern_detection.low: I need someone to point out the recurring structures in new material

pattern_detection.high: When I study examples, the underlying template usually jumps out at me
pattern_detection.low: When I study examples, I need the underlying template explained to me

logical_rigor.high: I want every term defined precisely before I use it in an argument
logical_rigor.low: I am comfortable using terms loosely if the general idea comes across

logical_rigor.high: I prefer proofs that spell out every logical step without gaps
logical_rigor.low: I prefer explanations that skip the obvious steps to keep the flow

contradiction_sensitivity.high: Conflicting statements in a text stand out to me as I read
contradiction_sensitivity.low: Conflicting statements in a text usually escape my notice while I read

contradiction_sensitivity.high: I catch it right away when a later chapter contradicts an earlier one
contradiction_sensitivity.low: I only notice when a later chapter contradicts an earlier one if I review

global_framing_need.high: I need to see the overall map of a topic before I learn the first detail
global_framing_need.low: I am happy to learn the first detail without seeing the overall map first

global_framing_need.high: I read the table of contents and summary before I start chapter one
global_framing_need.low: I jump straight into chapter one without checking the table of contents

cycle_architecture.high: I prefer a long lecture followed by one big practice session at the end
cycle_architecture.low: I prefer short bursts of teaching each followed by a quick practice check

cycle_architecture.high: I like to absorb a whole module before I test myself on any of it
cycle_architecture.low: I like to test myself after every few minutes of new material

attention_runway.high: I can stay locked on difficult material for an hour without a break
attention_runway.low: My mind starts to drift after about fifteen minutes on difficult material

attention_runway.high: I finish a dense chapter in one sitting without losing the thread
attention_runway.low: I have to put a dense chapter down and come back to finish the thread

warmup_latency.high: I need ten minutes of easy review before I can tackle hard new content
warmup_latency.low: I can tackle hard new content the moment I sit down to study

warmup_latency.high: I reread yesterday's notes for a while before starting today's lesson
warmup_latency.low: I dive straight into today's lesson without rereading yesterday's notes

fatigue_curve.high: My accuracy drops noticeably during the last third of a long study session
fatigue_curve.low: My accuracy stays steady from the start to the end of a long study session

fatigue_curve.high: Complex problems feel much harder at hour two than they did at hour one
fatigue_curve.low: Complex problems feel equally hard at hour two as they did at hour one

momentum_dependence.high: I need to see quick progress or I lose motivation.
momentum_dependence.low: I keep going even when progress feels slow at first.

momentum_dependence.high: Early wins help me stick with a new subject.
momentum_dependence.low: I don't need early success to stay interested in a topic.

interleaving_tolerance.high: I switch between topics during a study session.
interleaving_tolerance.low: I finish one topic completely before starting another.

interleaving_tolerance.high: Mixing different subjects keeps me engaged longer.
interleaving_tolerance.low: I prefer to focus on a single subject per session.

rush_tendency.high: I skim the instructions and start the task immediately.
rush_tendency.low: I read the instructions carefully before I begin.

rush_tendency.high: I pick the first answer that looks right and move on.
rush_tendency.low: I review all the choices before selecting an answer.

deliberation_depth.high: I think through the steps before writing an answer.
deliberation_depth.low: I go with my first instinct when answering questions.

deliberation_depth.high: I pause to consider different ways to solve a problem.
deliberation_depth.low: I use the first method that comes to mind.

session_rhythm.high: I study at the same time on most days of the week.
session_rhythm.low: My study times change constantly depending on my mood.

session_rhythm.high: I follow a fixed schedule for my learning sessions.
session_rhythm.low: I fit studying in whenever I have a random free moment.

reentry_cost.high: I need to re-read my notes before continuing after a break.
reentry_cost.low: I pick up right where I left off after stopping.

reentry_cost.high: After a day off, I review previous material first.
reentry_cost.low: I jump back in without reviewing old work.

stimulus_envelope.high: I can handle loud music and bright lights while learning.
stimulus_envelope.low: I need a quiet room with minimal distractions to focus.

stimulus_envelope.high: I stay focused even when my environment is chaotic.
stimulus_envelope.low: Any background noise breaks my concentration completely.

novelty_hunger.high: I get bored if the lesson format stays the same.
novelty_hunger.low: I prefer lessons that follow a familiar structure.

novelty_hunger.high: I look for new apps or methods every few weeks.
novelty_hunger.low: I stick with the same study tools for months.

retrieval_strength.high: I can explain a concept to someone else without looking at my notes.
retrieval_strength.low: I need to glance at my notes before I can explain a concept to someone.

retrieval_strength.high: Key ideas pop into my head when I sit down to write a summary.
retrieval_strength.low: I have to reread the chapter before key ideas come to mind for a summary.

recognition_recall_gap.high: Multiple-choice questions feel easy, but short-answer questions leave me stuck.
recognition_recall_gap.low: Short-answer questions feel just as doable as multiple-choice questions for me.

recognition_recall_gap.high: I recognize the correct term instantly in a list, but cannot say it on my own.
recognition_recall_gap.low: Naming the term from memory feels just as automatic as spotting it in a list.

decay_rate.high: Details from a lecture fade from my mind by the next morning.
decay_rate.low: Details from a lecture stay clear in my mind for several days.

decay_rate.high: I have to relearn vocabulary words every week because the old ones slip away.
decay_rate.low: Vocabulary words I learned months ago are still familiar without recent practice.

elaboration_benefit.high: Putting a concept into my own words makes it stick much longer.
elaboration_benefit.low: Rewording a concept in my own words does not help me remember it better.

elaboration_benefit.high: Explaining a topic out loud to myself helps me retain it for the test.
elaboration_benefit.low: Talking through a topic out loud does not improve how well I remember it.

mnemonic_receptivity.high: A catchy rhyme or acronym helps me lock in a list of steps for weeks.
mnemonic_receptivity.low: Rhymes or acronyms feel forced and I forget the list just as fast.

mnemonic_receptivity.high: Linking new terms to vivid mental images makes them easy to retrieve later.
mnemonic_receptivity.low: Creating mental images for new terms feels like extra work that does not pay off.

consolidation_need.high: I need a quick recap at the start of a study session to get oriented.
consolidation_need.low: I can jump straight into new material without reviewing the last session.

consolidation_need.high: A one-page summary sheet is essential for me to connect the week's ideas.
consolidation_need.low: I can connect the week's ideas in my head without a written summary sheet.

interference_susceptibility.high: Similar formulas like area and perimeter get mixed up in my head during a test.
interference_susceptibility.low: I keep similar formulas like area and perimeter straight without much effort.

interference_susceptibility.high: When two historical events share dates, I often swap their details by mistake.
interference_susceptibility.low: Shared dates between historical events rarely cause me to confuse their details.

enactive_encoding.high: I understand a science concept best after building a model or running the experiment.
enactive_encoding.low: Reading a clear explanation of a science concept is enough for me to understand it.

enactive_encoding.high: I learn a software tool faster by clicking through menus than by watching a tutorial.
enactive_encoding.low: Watching a tutorial teaches me a software tool just as fast as clicking through it myself.

perfectionism.high: I redo my notes until every page looks flawless.
perfectionism.low: I keep my notes messy if they still make sense.

perfectionism.high: I restart an essay if one paragraph feels off.
perfectionism.low: I fix the weak paragraph and keep writing forward.

productive_struggle.high: I keep trying different approaches before asking for help.
productive_struggle.low: I ask for a hint as soon as I feel stuck.

productive_struggle.high: I sit with a confusing problem for a while longer.
productive_struggle.low: I look up the answer quickly so I can move on.

confidence_calibration.high: My gut feeling about my score usually matches the result.
confidence_calibration.low: I am often surprised by how high or low my grade is.

confidence_calibration.high: When I feel sure I mastered it, the test confirms it.
confidence_calibration.low: I feel ready for the test but then miss easy questions.

error_driven_learning.high: Once I understand a correction, I stop making that error.
error_driven_learning.low: I keep making the same mistake even after it is explained.

error_driven_learning.high: I review my wrong answers so I do not repeat them.
error_driven_learning.low: I glance at the right answer and move to the next question.

self_monitoring.high: I can list exactly which concepts I need to review.
self_monitoring.low: I finish a chapter unsure of what I actually learned.

self_monitoring.high: I pause to check if I can explain the idea in my own words.
self_monitoring.low: I keep reading even when the material stops making sense.

strategy_awareness.high: I pick a specific study method based on the material.
strategy_awareness.low: I use the same study routine for every subject.

strategy_awareness.high: I switch to practice tests when rereading stops working.
strategy_awareness.low: I reread the textbook even when it does not help.

mastery_orientation.high: I keep exploring a topic until it clicks internally.
mastery_orientation.low: I stop studying once I can answer the practice questions.

mastery_orientation.high: I want to understand why the formula works, not just how.
mastery_orientation.low: I memorize the steps needed to get the right answer.

autonomy_preference.high: I choose my own resources and pace for a new topic.
autonomy_preference.low: I prefer a teacher to assign specific pages and deadlines.

autonomy_preference.high: I design my own project plan instead of following a template.
autonomy_preference.low: I work better when given a detailed checklist to follow.

identity_alignment.high: I work harder when a task feels like "something people like me do."
identity_alignment.low: Framing a task as "for people like me" does not change my effort.

identity_alignment.high: I stick with a tough subject if it matches how I see myself.
identity_alignment.low: Whether a subject fits my self-image does not affect my persistence.

emotional_engagement.high: I remember facts better when I care emotionally about the outcome.
emotional_engagement.low: How much I care about a topic does not change how well I recall it.

emotional_engagement.high: Details stick when I feel excited or anxious while learning them.
emotional_engagement.low: My emotional state while studying has no effect on what I retain.

near_transfer.high: I can tweak a method I just learned to solve a slightly different problem.
near_transfer.low: I get stuck when a problem differs even a little from the example shown.

near_transfer.high: After one example, I handle new variations of that problem type easily.
near_transfer.low: I need a separate example for every small variation of a problem.

far_transfer.high: I use ideas from one subject to solve problems in a totally different area.
far_transfer.low: What I learn in one class rarely helps me in unrelated classes or tasks.

far_transfer.high: A concept from a past hobby often helps me understand a new work challenge.
far_transfer.low: Skills I pick up in one setting usually stay stuck in that setting.

application_orientation.high: I lose interest if I cannot see a practical use for what I am learning.
application_orientation.low: I enjoy learning theory even when there is no obvious practical payoff.

application_orientation.high: I prefer tutorials that start with a real problem, not abstract definitions.
application_orientation.low: I like starting with clear definitions before seeing any real-world examples.

conceptual_bias.high: I need to understand why a method works before I use it confidently.
conceptual_bias.low: I learn best by practicing the steps until they become automatic.

conceptual_bias.high: I struggle with a procedure if no one explains the reasoning behind it.
conceptual_bias.low: I can follow a procedure well even if I do not grasp the theory.

prior_knowledge.high: I already know most key terms and core ideas before a course begins.
prior_knowledge.low: I usually start a course unfamiliar with the basic vocabulary and concepts.

prior_knowledge.high: I can explain the fundamentals of this subject to a beginner right now.
prior_knowledge.low: I would have trouble explaining the basics of this subject to someone else.

misconception_persistence.high: Old wrong ideas pop back up even after I learn the correct explanation.
misconception_persistence.low: Once I understand the right answer, my old confusion does not return.

misconception_persistence.high: I catch myself falling back on a debunked shortcut when I work quickly.
misconception_persistence.low: Corrected mistakes stay fixed and do not reappear under time pressure.

generation_effect.high: I learn more when I write out the answers.
generation_effect.low: I learn about as much when I read the answers.

generation_effect.high: I remember material better after explaining it in my own words.
generation_effect.low: I remember material about as well after reading it once.

retention_index.high: I can explain last week's lesson without checking my notes.
retention_index.low: I forget most of last week's lesson without checking my notes.

retention_index.high: After a month, I still remember the main points from class.
retention_index.low: After a month, I remember very little from class.

failure_response.high: When I get something wrong, I try another way.
failure_response.low: When I get something wrong, I put the task aside.

failure_response.high: A wrong answer makes me want to check and revise.
failure_response.low: A wrong answer makes me want to stop checking.

error_recovery_speed.high: I fix my mistake as soon as I notice it.
error_recovery_speed.low: I need several tries before I fix my mistake.

error_recovery_speed.high: When my first answer is wrong, I correct it right away.
error_recovery_speed.low: When my first answer is wrong, I need several tries before correcting it.

frustration_threshold.high: I stay with a difficult problem for a while.
frustration_threshold.low: I leave a difficult problem after a few minutes.

frustration_threshold.high: I keep trying when a question takes many attempts.
frustration_threshold.low: I move on when a question takes more than a few tries.

hint_dependency.high: I ask for a hint whenever a question feels hard.
hint_dependency.low: I try a hard question without asking for a hint.

hint_dependency.high: I use a hint to get started on most new exercises.
hint_dependency.low: I begin most new exercises without using any hint.

help_seeking.high: I ask someone for help when I get stuck.
help_seeking.low: I keep working alone when I get stuck.

help_seeking.high: I ask my teacher to explain an unclear step.
help_seeking.low: I stay quiet when a step does not make sense.

guessing_propensity.high: I give an answer even when I am not sure.
guessing_propensity.low: I give an answer only when I am sure.

guessing_propensity.high: I choose an option even when none seem right.
guessing_propensity.low: I leave my answer blank when none seem right.

scaffolding_fade.high: I can start working without examples once I understand the basics.
scaffolding_fade.low: I need examples for a while before I try the work myself.

scaffolding_fade.high: I try new problems quickly after seeing one worked example.
scaffolding_fade.low: I keep checking worked examples while I practice new problems.

notation_comfort.high: I use formulas and symbols comfortably while working through problems.
notation_comfort.low: Formulas and symbols make me uneasy when I work through problems.

notation_comfort.high: I can read formulas and symbols without needing each symbol explained.
notation_comfort.low: I need every symbol explained before I can read a formula.

brevity_preference.high: I want the shortest explanation that still makes the idea clear.
brevity_preference.low: I want the full explanation, including every useful detail and example.

brevity_preference.high: I prefer a quick summary before deciding whether to read more.
brevity_preference.low: I prefer reading the complete explanation before deciding what to explore.

repetition_tolerance.high: Repeating an idea helps me understand and remember it.
repetition_tolerance.low: Repeating an idea quickly makes me lose interest in the topic.

repetition_tolerance.high: I practice the same skill again until the steps feel automatic.
repetition_tolerance.low: Practicing the same skill again soon feels boring to me.

feedback_granularity.high: When I get feedback, I want each mistake explained in detail.
feedback_granularity.low: When I get feedback, I mainly need to know right or wrong.

feedback_granularity.high: I ask for comments about each step of my answer.
feedback_granularity.low: I ask only whether my answer is right or wrong.

feedback_tone_sensitivity.high: I need corrections phrased gently so I can keep trying.
feedback_tone_sensitivity.low: I can use blunt corrections and keep working without hesitation.

feedback_tone_sensitivity.high: I prefer feedback that starts with encouragement before suggesting changes.
feedback_tone_sensitivity.low: I prefer feedback that skips encouragement and goes straight to changes.

open_response_performance.high: I can explain my reasoning clearly in my own words.
open_response_performance.low: I choose multiple-choice answers more easily than open-ended responses.

open_response_performance.high: I prefer writing a full explanation instead of selecting one answer.
open_response_performance.low: I prefer selecting one answer instead of writing a full explanation.

dialogic_preference.high: I prefer questions that guide me toward finding the answer myself.
dialogic_preference.low: I prefer explanations that give me the answer and clear steps.

dialogic_preference.high: I prefer discussing ideas through questions instead of direct explanations.
dialogic_preference.low: I prefer direct explanations instead of discussing ideas through questions.

intrinsic_motivation.high: I read articles on topics just because they look interesting.
intrinsic_motivation.low: I read articles mainly when I need the information for something.

intrinsic_motivation.high: I watch documentaries on random subjects for fun on weekends.
intrinsic_motivation.low: I watch documentaries only when they relate to a goal I have.

extrinsic_reward_sensitivity.high: I put in extra study time when a gift card is offered.
extrinsic_reward_sensitivity.low: I study the same amount whether a gift card is offered or not.

extrinsic_reward_sensitivity.high: I finish optional assignments if they come with bonus points.
extrinsic_reward_sensitivity.low: I skip optional assignments even if they come with bonus points.

competitive_drive.high: I check the leaderboard to see if I moved up a spot.
competitive_drive.low: I ignore the leaderboard because my rank does not matter.

competitive_drive.high: I practice more when I know my score will be posted publicly.
competitive_drive.low: I practice the same amount whether scores are posted or not.

praise_sensitivity.high: I spend more time on the next task after a teacher says 'great job'.
praise_sensitivity.low: I spend the same time on the next task after a teacher says 'great job'.

praise_sensitivity.high: I re-read my essay when a peer leaves a positive comment.
praise_sensitivity.low: I move on from my essay even if a peer leaves a positive comment.

evaluation_anxiety.high: My mind goes blank on a quiz even though I knew the material.
evaluation_anxiety.low: I recall what I studied without trouble during a quiz.

evaluation_anxiety.high: My hands shake when I start a timed practice test.
evaluation_anxiety.low: My hands stay steady when I start a timed practice test.

boredom_susceptibility.high: I switch tasks after ten minutes if the reading feels dry.
boredom_susceptibility.low: I keep reading for an hour even if the material feels dry.

boredom_susceptibility.high: I stop a video tutorial if the speaker has a monotone voice.
boredom_susceptibility.low: I finish a video tutorial even if the speaker has a monotone voice.

persistence.high: I try a different strategy when my first approach fails.
persistence.low: I stop working on the problem when my first approach fails.

persistence.high: I come back to a difficult chapter after taking a short break.
persistence.low: I skip the difficult chapter and move to the next one.

social_framing.high: I remember the case study better because it followed a specific person.
social_framing.low: I remember the case study the same whether it follows a person or not.

social_framing.high: I pay closer attention when a math problem uses a character's story.
social_framing.low: I pay the same attention to a math problem with or without a story.

integration_tendency.high: When learning something new, I connect it with earlier lessons.
integration_tendency.low: When learning something new, I keep it separate from earlier lessons.

integration_tendency.high: I start each course by using what I learned before.
integration_tendency.low: I start each course without using what I learned before.

depth_breadth.high: I prefer learning one part of a topic deeply.
depth_breadth.low: I prefer learning many parts of a topic.

depth_breadth.high: I like exploring the details before getting the basic picture.
depth_breadth.low: I like getting the basic picture before exploring any details.

creative_extension.high: When given a school task, I like adding my own creative ideas.
creative_extension.low: When given a school task, I prefer clear steps and one answer.

creative_extension.high: I prefer practice questions that let me invent my own ending.

reading.passage: In 1815, Mount Tambora on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa erupted with catastrophic force. It was the most powerful volcanic eruption in recorded history, ejecting an estimated 160 cubic kilometers of ash, pumice, and sulfur gases into the stratosphere. The immediate blast killed over 10,000 people, but the global consequences were far deadlier. The sulfur aerosols formed a veil around the planet, reflecting sunlight and cooling the Earth's surface. The following year, 1816, became known as the "Year Without a Summer." Average global temperatures dropped by 0.4–0.7°C, causing widespread crop failures and famine across North America, Europe, and China. In New England, snow fell in June, and rivers froze in July. Food prices skyrocketed, triggering riots in European cities and mass migration in the United States. The eruption also inspired cultural works; confined indoors by relentless rain, Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein, and Lord Byron composed the poem Darkness. Tambora demonstrated how a single geological event can rapidly alter global climate and human history.

reading.passage: In 1854, a severe cholera outbreak struck the Soho district of London, killing over 600 people in just a few days. The prevailing medical theory held that diseases like cholera spread through miasma — foul-smelling air from decaying organic matter. Dr. John Snow, a physician and anesthetist, suspected otherwise. He meticulously mapped the locations of cholera deaths and discovered a striking cluster around the Broad Street water pump. Snow interviewed residents and found that most victims had drawn water from that pump, while workers at a nearby brewery — who drank beer instead of water — and inmates of a workhouse with its own well were largely spared. He convinced local authorities to remove the pump handle, and the outbreak quickly subsided. Later investigation revealed that the pump's well had been contaminated by a leaking cesspit from a nearby house where a cholera-infected baby's diapers had been washed. Snow's work demonstrated that cholera spread through contaminated water, not air, and pioneered the use of spatial analysis in epidemiology. Though his findings were initially resisted, they laid the foundation for modern public health practices and the germ theory of disease.

minilesson.title: Why the Sky Is Blue: Rayleigh Scattering
minilesson.intro: Have you ever looked up on a clear day and wondered why the sky wears a brilliant blue coat? The answer lies in how sunlight interacts with the gases in our atmosphere. It is a beautiful demonstration of physics happening right above our heads every single day.
steps: Sunlight enters atmosphere, hits gas molecules.
Shorter blue wavelengths scatter in all directions.
Eyes detect scattered blue light everywhere.
minilesson.why: Sunlight contains all colors, each traveling as waves of different lengths. Air molecules are much smaller than light wavelengths. They scatter shorter wavelengths (blue and violet) much more efficiently than longer ones (red and orange). This strong preference for scattering short waves, known as Rayleigh scattering, fills the sky with diffuse blue light.
minilesson.extra: Violet light scatters even more than blue, but our eyes are less sensitive to it, and the sun emits less violet. At sunset, light travels farther through air, scattering blue away and leaving reds and oranges to dominate the view.

problem.q: If Earth had no atmosphere, what color would the daytime sky appear to an observer on the surface?
options: Black
Blue
White
Red

minilesson.hint: Think about what happens to sunlight when there are no gas molecules to scatter it.
minilesson.explain: Without an atmosphere, there are no particles to scatter sunlight toward your eyes. The sky would appear black, similar to the view from the Moon, with the sun looking like a bright white disk against the darkness.
minilesson.connect: Why do astronauts see a black sky on the Moon even during the lunar daytime?

minilesson.title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
minilesson.intro: Turning an idea into a binding federal law is a deliberate, multi-stage process designed to prevent hasty decisions. It requires cooperation between both chambers of Congress and the President, ensuring broad consensus before a statute takes effect.
steps: Bill passes House and Senate in identical form.
President signs bill or Congress overrides veto.
Law is codified and enforced by agencies.
minilesson.why: The Framers created a difficult legislative process to protect liberty by preventing tyranny of the majority. Requiring bicameral approval and executive review forces compromise, slows emotional reactions, and ensures laws reflect a broad, deliberative consensus rather than fleeting passions.
minilesson.extra: Most bills die in committee; only a fraction reach the floor. Citizens can track legislation via Congress.gov to see real-time status, sponsors, and roll-call votes.

problem.q: What happens immediately after both the House and Senate pass a bill in identical form?
options: It goes to the President for signature or veto.
It is sent to the Supreme Court for review.
It becomes law automatically without the President.
It returns to committee for final amendments.

minilesson.hint: Remember the role of the executive branch in the checks and balances system.
minilesson.explain: After passing both chambers, the bill is enrolled and sent to the President. The President then has ten days to sign it into law or veto it; if vetoed, Congress can override with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
minilesson.connect: Think of a rule change at school or work—who had to approve it before it became official?

minilesson.title: How Compound Interest Grows Money
minilesson.intro: Compound interest is money earning money. When you deposit money in an account, the bank may pay you interest on the original amount and on interest it has already earned. Over time, those gains can build quickly. Regular deposits and time can help your money grow, but returns are not guaranteed, and fees or taxes may reduce what you keep.
steps: Deposit money and find an account that states its annual interest rate.
Let the account earn interest and add it to the account balance.
Repeat regularly, adding extra deposits whenever your savings plan safely permits them.
minilesson.why: Compound interest works because each new interest payment joins the principal. Future interest is then calculated on that larger balance, creating a cycle of earning and earning again. A longer time horizon can produce more growth because the balance has more opportunities to compound. The effect is strongest with higher rates, frequent compounding, and additional contributions.
minilesson.extra: Compare yearly and monthly compounding at the same rate. Annual percentage yield can show the effective yearly return after frequent compounding. Before investing, check fees, minimum balances, withdrawal rules, taxes, and whether rates can change.

problem.q: You deposit $1,000 at 10% annual interest. After one year, interest is $100. If that $100 stays in the account and earns 10% interest the next year, how much interest is earned in year two?

minilesson.hint: Consider whether the second year's interest is based only on the original deposit.
minilesson.explain: The first year's $100 interest is added to the $1,000 principal, making the new balance $1,100. At 10%, 10% of $1,100 is $110, so $110 of interest is earned during the second year.
minilesson.connect: Can you connect this to a savings goal by estimating how much earlier saving could help?

taste.a:
The water cycle continuously moves water between the sea, air, and land through three main processes: evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. Water evaporates from the sea into the air as vapor, condenses into clouds, and falls as precipitation onto land or sea, where it can evaporate again or flow back to the sea.

Example 1: On a sunny day, the Pacific Ocean absorbs heat. Surface water evaporates, rising as invisible vapor. The vapor cools at higher altitudes, condensing into tiny droplets that form cumulus clouds. Wind carries these clouds eastward. Over the Sierra Nevada, the air rises and cools further. Droplets merge and fall as snow. The snowpack melts in spring, feeding rivers that return water to the Pacific.

Example 2: In the Amazon Basin, afternoon heat causes massive evaporation from the rainforest canopy and the Atlantic moisture flowing inland. Water vapor rises rapidly, forming towering cumulonimbus clouds. These clouds release heavy rain within hours. Much of this rain is intercepted by the forest and transpired again, while the rest runs off into the Amazon River, which discharges it back into the Atlantic Ocean.
taste.b:
On a sunny day, the Pacific Ocean absorbs heat. Surface water evaporates, rising as invisible vapor. The vapor cools at higher altitudes, condensing into tiny droplets that form cumulus clouds. Wind carries these clouds eastward. Over the Sierra Nevada, the air rises and cools further. Droplets merge and fall as snow. The snowpack melts in spring, feeding rivers that return water to the Pacific.

In the Amazon Basin, afternoon heat causes massive evaporation from the rainforest canopy and the Atlantic moisture flowing inland. Water vapor rises rapidly, forming towering cumulonimbus clouds. These clouds release heavy rain within hours. Much of this rain is intercepted by the forest and transpired again, while the rest runs off into the Amazon River, which discharges it back into the Atlantic Ocean.

These examples show the water cycle in action: water continuously moves between the sea, air, and land through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. Water evaporates from the sea into the air as vapor, condenses into clouds, and falls as precipitation onto land or sea, where it can evaporate again or flow back to the sea.

taste.a: Igneous rocks form when molten material cools and solidifies. If cooling happens underground, the rock is intrusive and has large crystals; if it happens on the surface, the rock is extrusive and has fine grains or glassy texture. Sedimentary rocks form from sediment — fragments of older rocks, mineral crystals, or organic matter — that is compacted and cemented together, often in layers. They frequently contain fossils and may show ripple marks or mud cracks. Metamorphic rocks form when existing igneous, sedimentary, or other metamorphic rocks are changed by heat, pressure, or chemically active fluids without melting. This process can produce foliation, a parallel alignment of minerals, and new minerals such as garnet or kyanite. All three rock types are linked by the rock cycle: any rock can become another type through geologic processes.
taste.b:
Type | Origin | Key Features | Typical Examples
Igneous | Cooling and solidification of molten material (magma or lava) | Intrusive: coarse crystals (e.g., granite); Extrusive: fine grains or glass (e.g., basalt) | Granite, basalt, obsidian
Sedimentary | Compaction and cementation of sediment (rock fragments, mineral crystals, organic matter) | Layered; often contains fossils, ripple marks, mud cracks | Sandstone, limestone, shale
Metamorphic | Transformation of existing rock by heat, pressure, or chemically active fluids (no melting) | Foliation (parallel mineral alignment); new minerals such as garnet, kyanite | Schist, gneiss, marble

taste.a: Vaccines introduce harmless antigens that mimic pathogens. The immune system recognizes these, produces specific antibodies and memory cells, then clears the antigens. Later, if the real pathogen appears, memory cells rapidly launch a stronger, faster response, preventing illness.
taste.b: Vaccines work by presenting the immune system with harmless antigens — proteins or weakened/inactivated pathogens — that resemble dangerous microbes without causing disease. Immune cells such as dendritic cells capture these antigens and present them to helper T cells, which activate B cells to produce targeted antibodies and generate long-lived memory B and T cells. The antigens are then eliminated. Because memory cells persist for years, they can recognize the actual pathogen immediately upon future exposure, triggering a rapid, high-volume antibody response and cytotoxic T-cell attack that clears the infection before symptoms develop. This training effect is the foundation of adaptive immunity.

taste.a: Titus was a courier in the Roman Empire. He used its roads to carry messages quickly, while soldiers traveled along them to reach distant provinces and merchants used them to move goods. Supplies also moved over the roads. By connecting the provinces to Rome, the roads made tax collection and trade easier and helped spread Roman laws and customs to new regions. Titus could see that they were the empire's lifelines, keeping its vast territory connected and easy to govern.
taste.b: Roman roads served as the empire's lifelines, keeping its territory connected and easy to govern. They let couriers, soldiers, and messages travel quickly and allowed supplies and merchants' goods to move. By connecting the provinces to Rome, they made tax collection and trade easier and helped spread Roman laws and customs to new regions.
